en: One fascicle of the Continued *Zhengyuan Shijiao Lu* from the Year Yi-si of the Baoda Era of the Great Tang,
compiled by the Chan Master Hengan, a monk who retrieved scriptures at Bao’en Chan Monastery in the Right Street of the Western Capital.

Preface: I have heard that after Kāśyapa Mātanga entered Han China, the teachings of the Buddha began to spread throughout Zhina. Now, as we reach the sagely Tang dynasty, the era has reached its full fruition.
The Brahma scriptures flourish and abound within the oceanic treasury;
furthermore, during the reign of our Most August Emperor, who governs the entire realm,
in the eighteenth year of the Kaiyuan era, the year of Gengwu.
The śramaṇa Zhisheng of Chongfu Monastery in the Western Capital compiled the *Kaiyuan Catalogue of Śākyamuni’s Teachings* in twenty fascicles,
which was designated as the *Kaiyuan Record* of the canon.
In total, there are five thousand forty-eight fascicles comprising the sūtras, vinayas,
and śāstras of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, as well as the collected biographies of worthies and sages.
It comprises four hundred and eighty-one fascicles and is widely circulated in the world; furthermore,
it has passed through four successive dynasties.
From the reigns of Emperors Xuanzong, Suzong, Daizong,
and Dezong, until the tenth year of Emperor Dezong’s Zhenyuan era, the year of Jiashu (794 CE),
another sixty-five years elapsed.
During that time, seven Indian monks collaborated to propagate and translate the sūtras,
vinayas, and śāstras of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna traditions.
Including the supplementary texts from the Kaiyuan Catalogue, the Vinaya texts translated by Yijing,
the Mahābuddhanāmasūtra, the Bielu (Separate Transmissions), and so forth,
totaling one hundred and thirty-four works.
In two hundred and ninety-nine fascicles.
Compiled by the śramaṇa Yuánzhào of Xīmíng Monastery in the Western Capital, this is the *Continuation of the Kāiyuán Catalogue* in three fascicles.
Furthermore, in the fifteenth year of the Zhenyuán era, [it was completed].
By imperial decree, the *Zhenyuan shijiao lu* (Catalogue of Buddhist Teachings Compiled during the Zhenyuan Era) in thirty fascicles was compiled;
together with the texts translated by the seven preceding individuals and other Indian monks,
they comprise three hundred and thirty-two fascicles in total.
Including the previously mentioned Kaiyuan lu canon,
there are a total of five thousand three hundred and eighty fascicles,
comprising five hundred and ten bundles.
I have compiled these as the *Zhenyuan lu* (Zhenyuan Catalogue) and issued them for circulation; however,
since the time of the Jiangbiao region, one or two sections among them have remained unincorporated into the canon.
However, during the Dinchu year of the Tianyou era,
while residing in Jiangbiao,
I traveled to visit various famous mountains.
While seeking out spiritual friends and,
in addition to questioning them, perusing the Tripitaka,
he engaged in discussion with his fellow practitioners.
He recounted the circumstances of the Zhenyuan Canon;
Daoyou then opened his private storehouse and made a solemn vow to obtain this scripture.
I am about to return to the capital,
hoping to contribute to the Imperial transformation and bring eternal blessings to the state and the family.
Having secretly relied upon the Sagely Court and looked up to the power of Your Majesty’s wisdom,
in the second year of the Shengyuan era of the Great Tang,
I traveled far to pay homage at Mount Wutai;
since returning from the region west of the Passes,
I have transcribed and recorded the aforementioned collection of the *Zhenyuan lu* (Zhenyuan Era Catalogue) of the Tripitaka, including the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras.
In the third year of the Baoda era of the Great Tang,
he returned to the imperial court;
from the year Jiaxu of the Zhenyuan era until now, one hundred and fifty-two years have elapsed.
Subsequently, I was once again graced by the imperial favor of His Majesty the Emperor, who graciously granted my request for transcription and implementation;
an edict was issued to the relevant authorities to ensure it is permanently included within the various scriptural collections.
He further commissioned Qiao Kuangshun— Chao-san-da-fu serving as Shang-shu Jia-bu Yuan-wai-lang, Zhi-zhi-gao, Yun-qi-wei, and recipient of the purple-golden fish bag—
to compose a preface that precedes the main body of the scripture.
It not only provides benefit and profit for a single era,
but serves as a vessel for all time. Furthermore,
it was previously collected at the Sīta-kṣetra Monastery (Sīta-yuan) of Shengyuan Temple within the Imperial City.
One volume of the *Qianbo Manjusri Sutra* in ten fascicles was obtained;
it is also a translation by the Tripitaka Master Vajrabodhi included within the *Zhenyuan lu*,
yet it was omitted and not recorded in the *Zhenyuan zonglu*.
Having investigated the circumstances of the matter,
I request that it be deposited within this collection for cataloging and implementation.
Furthermore, there is one work in thirty fascicles titled *Yiqiejing yuandili*,
which was not included in the Zhenyuan Canon;
it is now likewise counted and placed hereafter.
Furthermore, Master Li’s *Huayan lun* (Treatise on the Avataṃsaka), one volume consisting of forty fascicles,
was presented for imperial inspection by Sengmian and Chang in the second year of the Shengyuan era.
The *Guangwen susu xiaogao huangdi* (Emperor Guangwen Susu Xiaogao),
with a preface composed by Sun Ji, the current Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites,
has been compiled within the Tripiṭaka; it excludes the number of scriptures contained in the *Kaiyuan lu*.
Now, according to the new comprehensive calculation, there are a total of one hundred and forty sections comprising four hundred and thirteen fascicles;

including the *Continued Catalogue of New Scriptures* in one fascicle, they comprise forty-three cases (*zhì*). The newly recorded titles of the scriptures and their catalogues are listed in full as follows. For detailed particulars—including those translated individually, collectively, or in combination—all are fully described in the thirty-fascicle *Zhengyuan Shijiao Lu*.
The Kaiyuan lu records that the canon consists of a total of one thousand seven hundred and sixty works,
comprising five thousand four hundred and eight fascicles.

Four hundred and eighty-one cases (zhi). Compiled by the śramaṇa Zhisheng of Xichongfu Monastery in the Western Capital, under imperial decree in the eighteenth year of the Kaiyuan era, the Gengwu year.
The Zhenyuan lu catalog records a total of one thousand two hundred and thirteen works,
comprising five thousand three hundred and ninety fascicles.
Five hundred and ten bundles. Compiled by the śramaṇa Yuánzhào of Xīmíng Monastery in the Western Capital during the year Wùyǐn (15th year of the Zhenyuán era), by imperial decree;
one hundred and thirty-seven new works have been added.

Together with three hundred and forty-three fascicles, including the *Qianbo jing* (Sutra of the Thousand Bowls), they comprise thirty bundles and some loose fascicles scattered among various bundles; furthermore, regarding both the old versions and the new translations, one should carefully examine the sequence of the translators.

The *Zhenyuan Pin-ci Lu* (Record of the Classification of Works from the Zhenyuan Era), one volume, thirty fascicles; combined in three bundles. The *Huayan Lun* (Treatise on the Avataṃsaka), one volume, forty fascicles; combined in four bundles. Newly compiled for inclusion in the Canon during the year Yisi of the Baoda era of the Great Tang. The *Xu Xinyi Zhenyuan Lu* (Continued Record of New Translations from the Zhenyuan Era), one volume; included in the same bundle as the *Xu Kaiyuan Lu* (Continued Record of the Kaiyuan Era) for new compilation and inclusion in the Canon. This concludes the *Xu Xinyi Zhenyuan Lu* held in the Canon.
A catalog of the sequence of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras;
and the number of fascicles for the *Sahasrabhakta-sūtra* and other texts, as observed and recorded through transcription.
In total, there are one hundred and thirty-nine works comprising three hundred and seventy-three fascicles, bound in thirty-nine bundles.

Included within these are the titles of the new scriptures, as well as the *Buddhanāmasūtra*, which was originally sixteen fascicles but has now been expanded to eighteen. Consequently, the grand total is increased by two fascicles. The old edition consisted of five thousand six hundred sheets, with twenty-eight lines per sheet; the new edition consists of six thousand three hundred and eighty sheets, with twenty-five lines per sheet. The catalog occupies one sheet of twenty-two lines. Furthermore, the forty-fascicle *Avataṃsaka-śāstra* is included, though its paper count is not yet accounted for here.
Once, he presented to the Emperor the newly translated Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras contained in the Zhenyuan lu,
as well as the Zhenyuan Catalogue and the Pincililu (Catalogue of Contents).
In total, there are one hundred and thirty-five works,
comprising three hundred and forty-three fascicles,
including the original petition for submission and the catalog of contents.
There are one hundred and thirty-two sections in total.
Among these, three sections are not included in the numerical catalog,
yet their number of fascicles remains as it was previously.
In total, there are now one hundred and thirty-five works:
one hundred and twenty-three Mahāyāna sūtras and dhāraṇī-recitation manuals.
Two hundred and thirty fascicles.
One work of the Mahāyāna Vinaya in one fascicle.
Two works of the Mahāyāna Śāstra in two fascicles.

Among the seven works in fifty fascicles listed as "remnants" in the Kaiyuan Catalogue translated by Yi Jing under the Hīnayāna Vinaya section, three fascicles were not found when the original texts were sought.
One work in three fascicles was subsequently added to the Kaiyuan Shijiao Lu.
In the tenth year of the Zhenyuan era (the Jiashu year), the śramaṇa Yuanzhao of Ximing Monastery in the Western Capital compiled this new revision by imperial decree, titled the Zhenyuan Catalogue.
*Shijiao lu* (Record of the Buddhist Teachings), one volume in thirty fascicles, compiled by the śramaṇa Yuánzhào of Xímíng Monastery by imperial decree in the sixteenth year of the Zhēnyuán era,
the Jǐmǎo year (799 CE). *Yīqièjīng yuánpǐn cìlù* (Catalogue of the Sources and Sequence of All Scriptures), one volume in thirty fascicles, compiled by the śramaṇa Cóngfàn of Yè Prefecture,
from the ninth year of the Dàzhōng era, the Yǐhài year (845 CE), until the first year of the Xiántōng era, the Gēn year (860 CE).

In the Year of the Dragon (*chén*), according to the *Zhēnyuán rùzàng lù* (Catalogue of Scriptures Entered into the Canon during the Zhenyuan Era), Volume One: First, regarding those works not counted in the *Zhēnyuán lù* but which have been transcribed and circulated, totaling nineteen fascicles across two sections: the *Mahābuddhanāmasūtra* is included in the *Chuán jí* (Collection of Transmissions) in sixteen fascicles, or eighteen fascicles;

it is appended to the Liang-era catalogue, though its details remain uncertain. Second, regarding those works that have been transcribed and circulated: [the above details]. [The text continues with further entries. 1. *Mahābuddhanāmasūtra*: Included in the *Chuán jí* collection; one section, sixteen fascicles, or eighteen fascicles; appended to the Liang-era catalogue; details unknown. 2. [Other entries follow... [End of entry] Note: The term *zhēnyuán* refers to the reign period of Emperor Dezong of the Tang dynasty (785–805). The *rùzàng lù* is a catalogue of Buddhist scriptures officially recognized for inclusion in the imperial canon. The *chuán jí* refers to a supplementary collection of texts that were widely disseminated but perhaps not formally cataloged in the primary registers. The "Liáng lù" refers to the *Dàtáng nánhǎi guǎnglì zhēnyuán shìjiè yīqiè jīngdiǎn zǒnglù*, compiled by Zhisheng during the Liang era of the Tang. The phrase "details unknown" (*wèixiáng*) indicates that the specific provenance or textual history of these works was not fully documented.
*The Separate Biography of the Author Shi Falin*, one volume in three fascicles, compiled by the śramaṇa Yancong;
included in the *Xin shiyi* (New Supplement) and recorded in the *Zhenyuan lu*. *The Sūtra of the Thousand Arms and Thousand Bowls of Mañjuśrī*, one volume in ten fascicles;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Vajrabodhi at Jianfu Temple in Chang’an during the twenty-eighth year of the Kaiyuan era; recorded in the *Shiyi*.
Newly included in the catalog and newly added to the canon: one volume of the *Huayan jing lun* (Treatise on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra) in forty fascicles, composed by the Venerable Li Tongxuan.

Submitted for imperial review by the monk Mianchang in the second year of the Shengyuan era, it was by imperial decree incorporated into the canon. The above items were received upon arrival and subsequently transcribed.
Furthermore, he newly compiled and included into the canon Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras,
as well as the *Zhenyuan lu* (Zhenyuan Catalogue) with its chapter arrangements,
the *Qianbo jing* (Sūtra of the Thousand Bowls), the *Huayan lun* (Treatise on the Avataṃsaka), and other works.
In total, there are one hundred and forty works,
comprising four hundred and thirteen fascicles,
arranged together in forty-three bundles.
The first section contains the detailed catalog entries.
The newly translated scriptures, vinayas, and śāstras of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna were recorded according to their sequence in the Zhenyuan Catalogue.

As listed below, these include the *Qianbo jing* (Thousand-Bowl Sūtra), the *Huayan lun* (Avataṃsaka-śāstra), and others; excluding the *Huayan lun*, the total count amounts to three hundred and thirteen fascicles.

The *Catalogue of the Tripiṭaka, Vinaya, and Śāstras Recorded during the Zhenyuan Era of the Great Tang*, including newly compiled entries: the *Newly Compiled Treatise on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra* in one volume, forty fascicles, together with its preface. This has been placed at the beginning because it records the dates of the sūtra’s submission. [There is also] a *Biographical Sketch* in one fascicle; as it appears either at the beginning of the treatise or after the final fascicle, it is not listed separately. Total: nine hundred sheets. [Drafted by] Zhong, Lei, and Qi. The above one work, forty fascicles, comprises four bundles.
This aforementioned treatise was composed by the Elder Li Tongxuan in the seventeenth year of the Kaiyuan era.
It was constructed in Daxian Village, Tongying Township, Yu County, to the northeast of Dayuan.
It became widely prevalent in the world during the second year of the Shengyuan era.
The monk Mianchang respectfully requested that it be included in the Imperial Canon.
[This was presented to] His Majesty, Emperor Gaozong of the Great Tang, styled Guangwen Sushu Xiaogao Huangdi.
He ordered ten copies to be made and had ten scrolls depicting the true likeness of the Elder Li transcribed,
which were then distributed throughout the various provinces.
It was included at the end of the Tripiṭaka;
furthermore, an imperial edict commanded Minister Sun Ji to compose a preface that was placed at the beginning of the treatise.
It is for this reason that it is now compiled here.
May there be no omissions or errors.
This is the Catalogue of Mahāyāna Sūtras, Dhāraṇī Recitation Methods, and Śāstras from the Tripiṭaka, compiled during the Zhenyuan era of the Great Tang, totaling one hundred and twenty-four works.

Two hundred and forty fascicles of scriptures translated during the Kaiyuan era of the Great Tang dynasty that have not yet been included in the ancient or modern catalogs consist of nine sections totaling twenty fascicles:

1. *The Mahāyāna Sūtra and Recitation Method of the Greatly Powerful Ucchuṣma Vidyārāja* (2 fascicles, or alternatively 3 fascicles; 35 sheets). 2. *The Essential Gate of the Spiritual and Magical Arts of the Great Perfect Dhāraṇī Spoken by Kṛtyāpasa-vajra* (1 fascicle; 5 sheets). 3. *The Method of the Hundred Transformations of the Prohibitions of Kṛtyāpasa-vajra* (1 fascicle; 3 sheets). The above three sections comprise five fascicles.
The original manuscript is currently extant.
It was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Ajitavinita (translated into Chinese as Wunengsheng) of Northern India at Anxi in the twentieth year of the Kaiyuan era.
Because the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmacandra presented these as tribute upon entering the court,
the aforementioned scriptures arrived at the capital; however,
they did not succeed in being included in the *Kaiyuan Lu*.
In accordance with an imperial edict, it was included in the Zhenyuan Catalogue:
*The Heart Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom, the Universal Treasury*, one fascicle, two sheets; this constitutes one work in one fascicle.
The original manuscript is currently extant.
It was translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Dharmachandra (translated into Chinese as Fáyùe), a native of East India,
in the twenty-sixth year of the Kaiyuan era.
Translated in Chang’an.
This single sutra does not differ in the slightest from the two ancient versions.
The one translated during the Yao Qin dynasty is titled the *Mahāprajñāpāramitāmahāvidyāmantra-sūtra*.
The translation by Xuanzang is titled the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*.
Its other meanings do not differ;
it is a different translation of the same original text as the two preceding sūtras.
There was only the main body (śarīra) [of the scripture], lacking the introductory section (nidāna) and the section on dissemination (pariṇāmanā).
Now, in the translation by Dharmacandra, all three sections are complete.
In accordance with the Imperial Decree, it was included in the *Zhenyuan Shijiao Lu*.

*The Method for Cultivating the Vairocana Samādhi of the Vajraśekhara Yoga*, one fascicle, fifteen sheets. Compiled by Qiao Kuangshun, Grand Master for Splendid Discourse (Chaosandafu), Acting Vice Director of the Department of Carriages in the Ministry of State Affairs, Knight of the Cloud Cavalry, and Recipient of the Purple Gold Fish Bag.

Preface to the Newly Acquired *Zhenyuan lu* Collection of Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna Sūtras, etc., Compiled by Imperial Decree. This preface is placed at the beginning of three sūtras: 1. *The Great Body Dhāraṇī of the Thousand-Handed and Thousand-Eyed Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva*, one fascicle, two sheets. 2. *The Greatly Vast, Perfect, and Unobstructed Heart-Dhāraṇī of the Compassionate Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva*, one fascicle, three sheets. 3. *The Secret Method of the Dhāraṇī of Acala*, one fascicle, eleven sheets. The above comprises four sections in four fascicles.
The original manuscript is still extant.
It was translated by the Tripitaka Master from South India, the Śramaṇa Vajrabodhi (translated into Chinese as Jīngāngzhì), during the nineteenth year of the Kaiyuan era and thereafter.
By imperial decree, he was included in the *Zhenyuan shijiao lu* (Zhenyuan Era Catalogue of Buddhist Teachings).

Later, during the reign of Emperor Dezong, he was posthumously granted the title of Kaifu Yitongsis and conferred the posthumous name "Great Propagator of the Teachings" (Dahongjiao) Tripiṭaka Master.
【Scriptures】 The above eight scriptures comprise ten fascicles in a single volume.
*The Scripture of the Thousand-Armed and Thousand-Bowl Mañjuśrī*, ten fascicles, one hundred and sixty sheets. This constitutes one collection of ten fascicles.

The preface at the beginning of that sūtra clearly records these details.

he sought out and transcribed various texts, which he has now brought with him to be included in the Zhenyuan Catalogue of the Tripiṭaka.
Within that collection, it was clearly observed that this sūtra had been omitted and not included in the Zhenyuan lu (Zhenyuan Era Catalogue).
It is stated that the details are fully recounted in the *Guangxing ji* (Extensive Record of Practice) by Vajrabodhi.
I had intended to visit [this place] and record my travels,
but as I was unable to fulfill this wish, I did not transcribe it.
Now, in the winter of the third year of the Baoda era of the Great Tang.
I humbly acknowledge the imperial grace bestowed upon me,
whereby the *Zhenyuan Catalogue* texts, which I have brought forth, were transcribed at Shengyuan Temple in the capital and compiled into the canon for circulation.
Furthermore, at the Tibetan Court (Zangxiangyuan) of Shengyuan Temple,
he saw another manuscript of this scripture and subsequently requested that it be included within the Zhenyuan Canon.
The Tripitaka Master Vajrabodhi previously translated the sūtra text,
which is included within the scriptures of this particular division (*kula*).
It is to be practiced according to the solar cycle.
Regarding the kingdom of Puzina,

It was permitted that this work be included within the Tripiṭaka;
furthermore, a formal report was submitted detailing the total number of volumes already compiled.
Now, fearing that as the years pass, it may again be lost as before, [I have taken this action].
